motion: In light of contemporary physics, should we accept that physical reality had a cause or beginning?

bridges.description: Establish that the available deductive and order-based arguments warrant accepting a cause or beginning for physical reality despite incompleteness in current physics.
Defend the principle that whatever begins to exist has some cause, and distinguish it from the proposed material-principle parallel.
Move from caused events and the rejection of infinite or circular dependence to an independent first cause.
Argue that an initially changeless first cause must be able freely to originate or withhold the first event, making it personal.
Maintain that events and changes remain real and causally relevant even if time, spacetime, or their metric is emergent or reducible.
Treat the high degree of physical order as evidence of an intelligent designer and therefore of a causal source of the ordered state.
Show that the record does not supply good reason to accept that physical reality had a cause or beginning, without undertaking to prove that it was beginningless or uncaused.
Argue that current physics and observations cannot determine the global past structure or establish a beginning of all physical reality.
Use the possibility of an initial nonmetric interval to block the inference from a non-infinite past or finitely many changes to a finite-length past and a beginning.
Use models in which temporal relations and events are grounded in a timeless physical substructure to challenge the claim that all physical reality began.
Argue that support for an efficient-causal principle has a material-principle counterpart, leaving no warrant to accept one while rejecting the other.
Question whether causation is fundamental or instead physically explained and applicable only within physical reality.
Distinguish the later ordering of a beginningless physical reality from a cause or beginning of physical reality as a whole.
